text:
Verses 91-105

(6:91) And they have not honored Allah with the honor that is due to Him when they say: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal.

Say: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought, a light and guidance for the people, which you make into parchment that you show while you conceal much? And you were taught what you did not know, (neither) you nor your fathers. Say: Allah. Then leave them sporting in their vain discourse.

(6:92) And this is a Book We have revealed, blessed, verifying that which was before it, and that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around her; and those who believe in the hereafter believe in it, and they keep a guard on their prayers.

(6:93) And who is more unjust than he who forges a lie against Allah, or says: It has been revealed to me; while nothing has been revealed to him, and he who says: I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed? And if you had seen when the unjust shall be in the agonies of death and the angels stretching out their hands: Give up your souls; today shall you be recompensed with an ignominious chastisement because you spoke against Allah other than the truth and (because) you showed pride toward His communications.

(6:94) And certainly you have come to Us alone as We created you at first, and you have lefiibehind your backs the things which We gave you, and We do not see with you your intercessors about whom you asserted that they were (Allah’s) associates in respect to you; certainly the ties between you are now cut offand what you asserted is gone from you.

(6:95) Surely Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone [to germinate]; He brings forth the living from the dead and He is the bringer forth of the dead from the living; that is Allah! How are you then turned away?

(6:96) Splitter of the dawn; and He has made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning; this is an arrangement of the Mighty, the Knowing.

(6:97) And He it is Who has made the stars for you that you might follow the right way thereby in the darkness of the land and the sea; truly We have elaborated the signs for a people who know.

(6:98) And He it is Who has produced you from a single soul, and (has given you) a dwelling-place and a repository; indeed We have elaborated the signs for a people who discern.

(6:99) And He it is Who sends down water from above, then We bring forth with it plants of every kind, then We bring forth from it green (foliage) from which We produce grain piled up (in the ear); and of the palm-tree, of the sheaths of it, come forth clusters (of dates) within reach, and gardens of grapes and olives and pomegranates, alike and unlike; behold the fruit of it when it yields

the fruit and the ripening of it; most surely there are signs in this for a people who believe.

(6:100) And they make the jinn associates with Allah, while He created them, and they falsely attribute to Him sons and daughters without knowledge; glory be to Him, and highly exalted is He above

what they ascribe (to Him).

(6:101) Originator of the heavens and the earth! How could He have a son when He has no consort, and He (Himself) created everything, and He is the Knower of all things.

(6:102) That is Allah, your Lord, there is no god but He; the Creator of all things, therefore serve Him, and He is Guardian over all things.

(6:103) No vision comprehends Him, but He comprehends all vision; and He is the All-Subtle, the All-Aware.

(6:104) Indeed there have come to you clear proofs from your Lord; whoever will therefore see, it is for his own soul, and whoever will be

blind, it shall be against himself, and I am not a keeper over you.

(6:105) And thus do We repeat the communications and that they may say: You have read; and that We may make it clear to a people who know.

Introduction

These verses have a moderate connection to the previous verses. The People of the Book denied the Prophet’s claim to a divine message by saying: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal (6:91). Thus the Qur’an

responds to them by reminding them of God’s revelation of scriptures to themselves. This links to the previous set of verses about God’s special guidance of the prophets, where part of it was that they were given a book. These verses start by arguing against the People of the Book. Then they mention that the greatest ẓulm (injustice, iniquity, wrongdoing) is to forge partners with God or commit injustice with regards to prophethood by either denying a true prophet or falsely claiming to be a prophet—as in the case of one who says: I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed (6:93). The verses then continue to talk about the end of such unjust people when they are overcome by death and are questioned by the angels who open their hands. The verses then present some signs of God’s unity in brief, and some of the best names of God and His sublime attributes.

(6:91) And they have not measured (qadarū) Allah with His due measure (qadrihi) when they say: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal. Say: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought, a light and guidance for the people, which you make into parchment that you show while you conceal much? And you were taught what you did not know, (neither) you nor your fathers. Say: Allah. Then leave them sporting in their vain discourse.

Qadr and qadar mean “the size of something in terms of smallness, largeness and the like.” The verbs qadartu and qaddartu are used when one measures and finds out the physical size, shape and quantity of something. However, the root has then been generalized and used also for non-physical things. For example the qadr of a person—in the sight of others and in

society—means how much people respect, regard and value that person. Usually, measures the limits of something is followed by providing a description of its qualities, which in turn results in knowledge about that thing. That is why qadr and taqdīr are also used, metaphorically, for “description of something” and “knowledge of something.” For example, qadara or qaddara al-shayʾ means “he described it.” It can also mean “he recognized it.” The lexical meaning of the root allows for all of these meanings.1

The holy essence of God cannot be embraced by any sense, imagination or intellect. Instead, only some of His holy attributes can ever be

known to a certain extent, and one can regard Him only as much as what one comprehends of His signs and actions. Hence, qadr in this verse can mean any of the above meanings.2 In other words, what is mentioned in this verse—And they have not measured Allah with His due measure—can mean any of the following: (1) They did not respect and regard God as He deserves to be respected. (2) They did not describe Him as He deserves to be described. (3) They have not known Him as He deserves to be known. The verse by itself can be interpreted according to any of these three meanings, or according to all of them, where one meaning would be an implication of another. However, we should also interpret the verse given the theme of the previous verses and in relation to them. The above verses talked about God’s guidance of His prophets, which entailed that they were given the book, judgment and prophethood [6:89]. They referred to His complete care in maintaining the message of truth and the bounty of guidance amongst the people throughout history, generation after generation [6:89]. Given this thread of meaning, the first interpretation is the most plausible, because denying God’s revelation [of scriptures to His prophets in order to guide humankind] would be disregarding and underestimating His value. Such denial entails that God is not a Lord Who

1 Here qadara and qaddara (or qadr and taqdīr) are synonymous and are both transitive. (Trans.)

2 Three main meanings were discussed above for qadr: (1) respect, regard, value; (2) description; and (3) knowledge. (Trans.)

cares for the affairs of His servants, Who has neglected to guide them to their goal of happiness and salvation.

The first interpretation is also confirmed by the usage of the same expression in the following verses: And they have not measured Allah with His due measure; but the whole earth shall be in His grip on the Day of Resurrection and the heavens rolled up in His right hand; glory be to Him, and may He be exalted above what they associate (with Him) (39:67); Surely those whom you call upon besides Allah cannot create a fly, though they should all gather for it, and should the fly snatch away anything from them, they could not take it back from it; weak are the seeker and the sought. And they have not measured Allah with His due measure; most surely Allah is Strong, Mighty (22:73-74). These verses mean that the power and might of God on the one hand, and the weakness and abasement of others on the other hand, necessitate that His honor and value should not be downgraded such that He is set equal to what they worship besides Him, whereby they equally consider Him and their idols to be lords and gods. Therefore, the first meaning is most relevant, although the other two meanings are also possible. Some exegetes have said that And they have not measured (qadarū) Allah with the measure (qadr) that is due to Him means that “they have not ascribed the power that He deserves to Him.” This is the least likely meaning given the theme and context of the verse. The verse has qualified this statement—that they have not measured Allah with His due measure—by adding: when they say: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal. This shows that what is meant by their lack of regard and honor for God is that they denied God having sent any revelation or scripture to a human being. This implies that if someone is to be accepted as a god and lord, he must send revelation and scripture to guide the people to the straight path which leads them to their happiness in this world and the hereafter. This is what the verse claims.

God then provides two arguments to prove this claim: (1) Say: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought… (6:91); and (2) And you were taught what you did not know, (neither) you nor your father (6:91). The first argument draws on the revelation of divine books upon prophets whose prophethood has been otherwise established by the evident miracles that they brought. This argument is based on the continuity and preservation of God’s guidance among the people by means of the prophets from Noah onwards. This guidance is what God described in the verses above, from: And when Abraham said to his father Azar… (6:74) to: it is nothing but a reminder to the nations (6:90).

The second argument refers to the presence of certain divine teachings and laws among humans, which they could not have ever arrived at

on their own. The human being is a social creature with an intellect and certain emotions that can lead it to seek its gain, avoid its loss, and acquire what it needs for its life, such as food, shelter, clothes and sex. These all fall under the category of material enjoyment, which is what humankind readily finds given its animal nature. However, divine teachings, noble moral virtues, and the legal codes which put those teachings and virtues into practice are not things that humankind can achieve by its collective reason. How can collective reason ever arrive at such teachings? The role and function of collective human reason is to guide people to utilize every means and instrument possible to fulfil their earthly needs and achieve their goals regarding food, drink, sex, clothes, shelter and so on. It also helps every individual to break any resistance that stops him from his personal enjoyment if he can—or, if that is not possible, to cooperate with others toward their common interest with an equitable distribution. This is why humankind is social, as we explained in our discussion

of prophethood under the verse: (All) people are a single nation; so Allah raised prophets… (2:213).1 Below we shall clarify this further, by God’s will. In short, taking its different aspects into consideration, this verse— And they have not measured Allah with His due measure (6:91)—states that God shall necessarily guide humankind to the straight path and a happy end by sending a book and revelation to some individuals. The verse provides two proofs for this conclusion: (1) there are already such books of guidance that God has sent; and (2) there exist certain divine teachings among humankind that cannot be a result of their collective reason.

Say: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought, a light and guidance for the people, which you make into (tajʿalūnahu) parchment (qarāṭīs) that you show while you conceal much?: The common recitation of the verse is with tajʿalūnahu in second person (that is, “which you

make into…”), where the audience would certainly be the Jews. However, the word has also been recited as yajʿalūnahu in third person (that is,

1 In other words, humankind is social by necessity. One cannot achieve all of one’s needs and wants alone, so people have no choice but to live and work together in the way of their mutual interest. (Trans.)

“which they make into…”). In this case, the audience—in Who revealed the Book?—would be either the Jews or the polytheists of Arabia. Thus has been said.

Qarāṭīs is the plural of qirṭās (parchment, paper, sheet). This part of the verse can be interpreted in two ways: (1) you place the book in parchment by writing on it; or (2) you make the actual book out of parchment,

meaning that you convert the book into the form of parchment which has writing on it. In other words, the term “book” may refer to two things: (1) the letters that are written; and (2) the parchment or papers on which the letters are written.1

Say: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought: Here the verse responds to their claim: when they say: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal (6:91). The verse does not explicitly identify who made this claim, but the particularities of the answer leave no doubt that it is addressed to the Jews, which means that they are the ones who said: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal (6:91). There are three reasons for this. (1) The verse brings in the book of Moses as evidence to argue against those who made this claim. Such an argument would not make sense against the polytheists because they did not believe in Moses’ book as a scripture that had been revealed by God. The People of the Book, on the other hand, believed in it. (2) The verse criticizes them for making this book into parchment that shows some but conceals much. This was a specific quality of the Jews, not the polytheists. (3) The subsequent part of the verse says: And you were taught what you did not know, (neither) you nor your fathers. Clearly the Jews would be the relevant audience of this straightforward statement, not the polytheists or the Muslims. We shall discuss this part of the verse further below, if God wills.

One problem is that the Jews believed in the prophethood of God’s prophets up to Moses, and in the revelation of divine books such as the Torah and other scriptures. Hence, it would not make sense for them to say, Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal (6:91), because it would contradict their fundamental beliefs.

The answer is: Even though this statement contradicts their system of

1 According to the first meaning, the word fī(in, into) is assumed as an implied omitted preposition, and “book” refers to the letters or concepts that are contained in the parchment. According to the second meaning, “book” refers to the very parchment. (Trans.)

beliefs, they might have still said it because of one of the following considerations: (1) out of their intense animosity against Islam; (2) in order to

entice the polytheists against the Muslims; or (3) in response to a question from the polytheists about the truth of the Prophet’s claim that God has revealed the Qur’an to him. Indeed they preferred the polytheists among Arabs over Muslim monotheists by saying: These [polytheists] are better guided in the path than those who believe (4:51). Thus they preferred the defilement of polytheism over the purity of monotheism, even though their own religion was based on monotheism. They were such that God says about them: Have you not seen those to whom a portion of the Book has been given? They believe in idols and false deities and say of those who disbelieve: These are better guided in the path than those who believe (4:51). They made an even more foolish statement than this out of enmity against the Christians by saying that Abraham was a Jew. Thus God revealed: O People of the Book! Why do you dispute about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed till after him; do you not then understand?... Abraham was not a Jew nor a Christian but he was (an) upright (man), a Muslim, and he was not one of the polytheists (3:65-67). Likewise, the Qur’an has narrated other statements from them that contradict their established principles. It is quite possible for people with

such conduct and behavior to deny the revelation of scriptures to human beings altogether out of some evil consideration and disposition. It is perceivable that such people would deny a truth that would be harmful and costly to them, or preach a falsehood that would be beneficial and profitable to them.

Another objection raised by some exegetes is that the Qur’an did not address the People of the Book in its Meccan chapters. When the Prophet was in Mecca before his migration to Medina, his religious call was directed at the polytheists because they were the people living there and causing trouble for Islam.

The answer is: This point does not mean that the People of the Book were lefiiaside in Mecca altogether. There are a few reasons for this: (1) Islam claimed from day one to be a universal religion and made its call to all people. The Qur’an was sent as a reminder for all nations from the beginning. (2) The polytheists [in Mecca] and the People of the Book [in Arabia] were neighbors; they used to meet and interact with each other consistently. (3) Some Meccan chapters mention the People of the Book, and there is no clear evidence to show that these verses were revealed later in Medina. For example God says: And do not dispute with the followers of the Book except by what is best, except those of them who act unjustly

(29:46); And for those who were Jews We prohibited what We have related to you already, and We did them no injustice, but they were unjust to themselves

(16:118). Similarly, Chapter 7 (al-Aʿrāf) mentions a series of aberrations committed by the Israelites even though the chapter is Meccan. (4) The call to Islam was made several years before the migration and there were many Jewish and Christian communities in the Arabian Peninsula at the time. It is very unlikely that this call did not reach them during this entire period, or that it reached them but they did not respond to it—whether positively or negatively. After all, a community of Muslims migrated at that time to Ethiopia and recited the Meccan Chapter 19 (Maryam) to the people there, which talks about the story of Jesus and his prophethood. Another objection raised by some exegetes is that this entire chapter—that is, Sūrah al-Anʿām—was revealed to argue against the polytheists concerning God’s unity. All of the addresses made in the chapter are

directed to them, which leaves no grounds for saying that the pronoun “they”—in when they say: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal

(6:91)—refers to the Jews. Rather, it certainly refers to the Arab polytheists, because this verse is in a series of verses which talk about them, as

opposed to the Jews of whom there was no mention in the chapter. We cannot assume that this one verse is an exception to the flow, theme and context of the chapter from its beginning up to this point—and afterwards until the end. There is no rational evidence or authenticated narration to support this interpretation. Hence, it is best to prefer the recitation of yajʿalūnahu in the third person, referring to the Jews who made the book into parchment. This would be a reference to the Jews while addressing the Arab polytheists.

The answer is: It is true that the previous verses argue against the polytheists, but they do not argue against them per se, as specific individuals. Whenever the Qur’an addresses a person or group, it addresses them

because of a specific quality in them. Otherwise, the Qur’anic addresses are never personal. In this case, the chapter addresses the polytheists because of their defiance against the truth and their rejection of the principal components of the religious call, which are monotheism, prophethood, and

the afterlife. In light of this point, the audience of these verses would be anyone who denies all or some of these principal beliefs. Thus it is perfectly compatible with the theme and flow of the chapter to describe some of the aberrations of the Jews if these aberrations necessitate the rejection of prophethood and revelation of scripture. This would be completely consonant with the deviations of the polytheists who denied the principal beliefs of God’s religion, even though it pertains to a community other than the polytheists and idol-worshipers. Perhaps the Jews used to teach this to the polytheists in order to cause mischief. There are some historical accounts saying that sometimes the polytheists used to ask the Jews

about the Prophet’s message, and sometimes they would even send entire delegations [to Medina] to discuss this issue with the Jews.1 In addition, there are two statements in the verse that cannot be properly addressed to anyone other than the Jews: (1) And you were taught what you did not know, (neither) you nor your fathers; and (2) Say: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought, a light and guidance for the people.

Some exegetes have responded the above objection as follows: Even though the polytheists did not believe in the Torah as a divine book, they nevertheless knew that the Jews followed the Torah as something that was revealed to Moses. This knowledge and familiarity suffices for the sake of the argument here.

However, the idea that the polytheists knew the Jews to be followers of the Torah of Moses cannot be a satisfactory explanation of the verse because the mere knowledge of this does not make it binding on the person to accept the Torah as God’s revelation, especially that the verse describes it as a light and guidance for the people. Believing that it has been revealed by God is not the same as knowing that the Jews claim this. Only the former would explain the verse, not the latter.

If the verse is recited with yajʿalūnahu [in third person], then it should be interpreted as a rhetorical shifiiofiaddress; otherwise the rest of the verse is directed at the Jews [in second person]: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought… And you were taught what you did not know, (neither) you nor your fathers (6:91).

Here is a summary of how one of the exegetes has accommodated both recitations [that is, tajʿalūnahu and yajʿalūnahu] in order to show that there is no problem in the verse being addressed to the polytheists:

1 This was at a time when the Jews were predominantly in Medina, and the Prophet and the polytheists were in Mecca. (Trans.)

The verse was initially revealed in a Meccan chapter with “which they make into parchment” (yajʿalūnahu) in the third person, as recited by Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmrw. This was an argument addressed to the polytheists in Mecca. They were denying revelation on the account that it is unlikely for God to speak to a mortal, yet they admitted to the book of Moses and would send delegations to Jewish scholars, acknowledging them as followers of the first divine book who know the stories of the prophets. That is why God told His Prophet to argue against these people who have not measured Allah with His due measure when they say: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal. For example they used to say: What! Has Allah raised up a mortal to be a messenger? (17:94). The Prophet was ordered to tell them: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought as a light—which illuminated the darkness of disbelief and polytheism which the Children of Israel had inherited from the Egyptians—and as guidance for the people, meaning those who learnt divine laws and rituals through the Torah. As a result, the Israelites were followers of the Torah’s light and guidance until they disagreed about it and they neglected a portion of what they were reminded of (5:13). Hence, due to following their own desires and interests, they make it into parchment that they show if it serves their interests, and of which they conceal much that goes against their desires. Apparently this is how the verse was recited in Mecca and also in Medina, until the incident where Jewish scholars [in Medina] concealed the law of lapidation [in favor of a married person who has committed adultery]. Likewise, they concealed the news about the coming of the Prophet in the Torah, to the point that some of them said: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal, just as the polytheists had said it before them—assuming that the accounts of these events are authentic. Then it makes sense that God inspired His Messenger to recite these sentences in presence of the Jews and address them [in the second person]: which you make into parchment that you show while you conceal much, without abrogating the initial recitation [in third person]. Nor does this ruin the consistent flow of the previous verses [because the second recitation belongs

to an event in Medina that was independent of the previous verses]. This is a plausible explanation based on the above-mentioned events, which allows for both recitations without requiring any contrivance. It answers all of the problems and objections that the exegetes have raised against the recitation of both versions of the verse.

However, even if we assume this possibility, the following problems still remain unanswered:

(1) It does not make sense to argue against the polytheists [in Mecca] through something that they did not believe in.

(2) It does not make sense to address a non-Jewish audience [in Mecca]: And you were taught what you did not know, (neither) you nor your fathers (6:91) as we discussed above.

(3) There is no reason to interpret “people” in a light and guidance for the people as the Jews alone.

(4) By admitting that the Jews in Medina said, Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal, the exegete is conceding and falling into what he was trying to avoid.

(5) Moreover, there is no proof for the claim that God “inspired” His Messenger to recite the verse a second time to the Jews [in Medina] as: which you make into parchment that you show while you conceal much [this time in second person]. W hat does “inspiration” mean here? (a) If it means a new revelation, with the difference that the verse was first revealed in the third person and then again in the second person, then it would mean that the verse was revealed twice: the first time it was revealed as part of the chapter, and the second in Medina without being part of the chapter.1 (b) If “inspiration” does not mean revelation through Gabriel, then it would not be part of the Qur’an, and its recitation would not be a recitation of the Qur’an.2 (c) It could means that God made His Messenger to understand somehow that this verse—which was revealed in Mecca—can be recited in both the second person and the third person, meaning that both recitations are correct and intended by God. This view is held by those who

claim that all the different recitations of the Qur’an were either recited by the Prophet or recited to him [with his consent]. However, this view clearly suffers from all of the problems that we listed above.

It should be noted that the above discussions are based on the assumption that the verse was revealed in Mecca. Otherwise, if the verse was

revealed in Medina [after the rest of the chapter] then most of the above issues would not be applicable.

… And you were taught what you did not know, (neither) you nor your fathers…: This sentence is not about ordinary knowledge of what is

1 This is obviously not the case and not claimed by anyone. (Trans.)

2 This contradicts an assumption behind the entire discussion above. (Trans.) beneficial and what is harmful in human life, which can be learnt through the faculties that humans generally have, such as the physical senses, imagination and reason. Instead, the knowledge that “they were taught which neither they nor their fathers knew” should be interpreted in light of the verse’s argument. The verse’s claim is that an implication of being a god is to guide humankind to their happiness by sending revelation and scripture to some of them. However, there is no relevance between this conclusion and the ordinary forms of knowledge that people can acquire through means that are already built in them. Similarly, the verse is not about God making people know what they did not know previously, as indicated by verses like: And He gave you hearing and sight and hearts

(16:78) and: HeWho taught (to write) with the pen; Hetaught man what he knew not (96:4-5). The context of the verse does not support this meaning. Hence, the verse is about extraordinary teachings that cannot be acquired through the cognitive capacity and instruments of humans in general. This is naught but what God has revealed to His prophets and His carriers of revelation, whether in the form of scripture or not. This knowledge consists of religious beliefs, laws, and codes of conduct that are not accessible through the normal means that are available to humans. This should clarify that the audience here—in And you were taught what you did not know…—are not the polytheists. They did not admit to possessing any clear share of prophetic teachings and divine laws. Even the pieces that they had inherited from the prophetic traditions of their forefathers were not things that they acknowledged; hence the verse cannot set these teachings as a basis for argument. Rather, God has described

them as being ignorant, where He says: And those who have no knowledge say: Why does not Allah speak to us? (2:118).

Given the above, this sentence cannot be addressed to the polytheists. Nor can it be addressed to the Muslims, because of the following reasons: (1) The verse involves a tone of debate and a theme of argumentation. If this sentence were directed at the Muslims, then it would be a parenthetical remark aside from the context of argumentation, while there is no clear reason to have such an aside. (2) That would entail a shifiiofiaudience— from Who revealed the Book which Moses brought to another audience in and you were taught…—while there is no clear indication for such a shif , not to mention that it would be confusing. Hence, the sentence is directed to neither the polytheists nor the Muslims, but to the Jews who are the audience of the first part of the verse.

The Jews claimed that Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal, either out of animosity or in order to cause mischief. In this verse God argues against them in two ways:

(1) He points out their belief in the Torah as a book that Moses brought as a light and guidance for the people. This contradicts their claim that Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal. This is a destructive argument by contradiction. God then goes on to criticize them for breaking this book into pieces, of which they show some but conceal much.

(2) He tells them: “You were taught things that were not in your capacity to learn on your own, nor was it in the capacity of your fathers to learn

and hand down to you.” These are things like religious beliefs, moral virtues, and legal codes and rules which are meant to settle disagreements in

human societies by giving them the best order, balance and organization. These teachings, especially the legal codes, are things that human beings cannot acquire through their own intellection. It is true that they can acquire some general religious beliefs concerning God’s unity, prophethood and the hereafter, as well as an overall understanding of moral

virtues, but this does not suffice to establish these teachings in human societies. Mere knowledge of something is different from its practice and its widespread implementation at the social level. The strong drive to enjoy material pleasures and the natural instinct to employ everything in order to fully exercise one’s desires and acquire one’s cravings leave no room for humankind to search for the treasures of divine realities and gnosis that are latent in their innate nature (fiṭrah). Thus these realities remain buried and do not become a foundation for human life. This is especially the case if this sense of materialism becomes a dominant trend and establishes a foothold in the entire society. Then the society becomes a closed setting and environment that limits the people to material enjoyment, without any opening for the light of human virtues to penetrate it. Any spiritual values and moral virtues inherited by this society will gradually disappear in such an environment, until the entire society turns into a primitive animalistic society as we observe in the advanced societies today, which have plunged into materialism and submitted to sensual pleasures. Thus every second of their life is occupied by such matters and they are completely inattentive of the hereafter and spiritual matters due to being totally engaged in the life of this world. This has blocked them from any thought or contemplation about how to achieve a happy eternal life.

There is no historical record of a ruler or politician in any nation or community who called its subjects to moral human virtues, pure divine teachings and the way of taqwá (Godwariness, self-restraint, piety) and servitude (ʿubūdiyyah) [to God]. In case of totalitarian rulers, their sole concern is to keep themselves in power and maintain their reign. And in case of collective governments such as democracies and the like, their greatest achievement is to organize the society according to what the majority desires—irrespective of that being a virtue or a vice; whether it is in line with true happiness as judged by sound reason or not. Sometimes these nations contravene certain spiritual values and noble human virtues which still remain in name among the people, and which are valued

and respected by the innate human nature—such as justice, modesty, honesty, benevolence, philanthropy, and kindness to the disadvantaged. When they want to violate these values, they interpret them according to their own course of action and common practices, as we can see with our own eyes today.

In short, our collective reason and material rationality—which rule our societies—cannot lead us to these divine teachings and spiritual virtues, the names of which have always been present in human societies, and the meanings of which people have ever cherished—despite all differences of opinion and varieties of culture. After all, there is a far distance between clinging to the earth and rising from matter and materiality toward the heaven.

What exists is only traces and remainders of religious calls which go back to the movements and struggles of the prophets to spread the call of truth, disseminate monotheism, and guide humankind to their true felicity in this life and the next. We owe these guidelines to God’s teaching through revelation and scriptures.

… And you were taught what you did not know, (neither) you nor your fathers…: This statement argues against the Jews and refutes their claim that: Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal (6:91). The argument is that you have some beneficial knowledge that you have not acquired yourselves, nor have you inherited from your forefathers. Rather, you were taught these through another means, which is the way of revelation and scripture sent from God upon some human being. Therefore, God has sent some true teachings—including religious beliefs and legal codes—upon some mortal. The Jews had indeed a large share of these teachings which they had inherited from their prophets and the book of Moses.

Even though the verse first talks about the Book which Moses brought specifically, the subsequent part does not say, “you were taught by it” or “God taught you through it.” Instead, it says: you were taught without qualifying it by the Torah. This, along with our explanation above, shows that

this part of the verse—and you were taught what you did not know—refers to any religious belief and law that is rooted in revelation and scripture in an absolute sense, not only the teachings of Torah as some exegetes have suggested. The unconditional text of the verse does not support such a restriction of meaning.

The verse says, you were taught in the passive voice. According to some exegetes, this better proves the verse’s objective because identifying the subject here would make the argument more like a vicious circle. The verse is effectively saying: “Among what you know there is some knowledge which you did not acquire by yourselves or through your fathers.

Who has taught you these?” The verse then says, “Allah” as the answer to both of the questions in this verse.

… Say: Allah. Then leave them sporting in their vain discourse: When the answer to some question is obvious and undoubtable, the inquirer does not wait for the inquired to respond, but proceeds to answer it himself. That is why God orders His Prophet to take on the task of answering by telling him: Say: Allah. It means God is the One Who revealed the Book which Moses brought, and the One Who taught you whatyou did not know, (neither) you nor your fathers.

The claim that Allah has not revealed anything to a mortal is vain and frivolous speech. Only those who take the truth as an object of sport and entertainment would make such a claim. This is especially true if the speakers are Jews who believe in the Torah of Moses and take pride in having knowledge of revelation and scripture. That is why God orders His Prophet to leave them with their affair: then leave them sporting in their vain discourse.

(6:92) And this is a Book We have revealed, blessed, verifying that which was before it, and that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around her; and those who believe in the hereafter believe in it, and they keep a guard on their prayers.

The last verse established the following points: (1) An implication of being a god is to send revelation upon a subset of human beings, which are called prophets. (2) There have been some true scriptures such as the Torah of Moses. (3) There is knowledge of other things that humankind has been taught, which only trace back to divine revelation and supernatural teachings. This verse continues the discussion by adding that this

Qur’an is also a divine book which God has sent, just like the other divine scriptures. The verse’s evidence for this claim is that this Book has the same qualities that are found in other books sent from God.

Given the above, the following points should be clear: (1) The theme of the verse is to identify God as the Sender of the Qur’an. The verse is not primarily concerned with the receiver of the Qur’an. That is why it says: a Book We have revealed, without saying, “We have revealed to you”—unlike other verses such as: (It is) a Book We have revealed to you abounding in good that they may ponder over its verses (38:29). (2) The qualities mentioned for the Book—in blessed, verifying—serve as reasons to prove it as

God’s revelation. To be more precise, they are not proofs, but they are signs and indications (amārāt) of a book that has been sent by God.

One indication of such a book is that it is blessed (mubārak), meaning that God has placed abundant and sustainable good in it. It guides the

people to that which is most upright (17:9) and: With it Allah guides him who will follow His pleasure into the ways of safety (5:16). It benefits the people in this world by resolving their disputes, giving them strength, uniting them, abolishing animosity from their hearts and rancor from their souls, spreading peace and security among them, making their lives prosperous and enjoyable, enlightening them against ignorance and every vice, and bringing them under the shade of true happiness. It also benefits them in the hereafter through great reward and eternal bliss.

This book could not have any of these blessings had it not been sent from God. For example, it could be a human fabrication made as a snare to deceive and entrap the people. It could be a satanic impression or an appealing imagination of one’s ego which one takes to be the word of God and divine revelation, while that is not the case. Either way, none of these divine blessings and abundant benefits could accrue from any other book, because the path of evil does not lead its traveler to anything but evil, and perfection never grows out of corruption. God says: Surely Allah does not guide one whom He leads astray (16:37); And Allah does not guide the iniquitous people (61:5); And as for the good land, its vegetation springs forth (abundantly) by the permission of its Lord, but (as for) that which is inferior (its herbage) comes forth but scantily (7:58).

Another indication of such a book is that it speaks the truth and verifies the previous scriptures which were truly sent by God.

Another indication of such a book is that it fulfills God’s objective vis-à-vis His servants, which is to guide them to happiness in both this world and the next. He achieves this objective through warning them and sending revelation to them, as we see in the next part of the verse. … and that you may warn (li-tundhira) the Mother of Cities (umm al-qurá) and those around her…:Umm al-Qurá (lit. “mother of cities, metropolis”) refers to the holy precinct of Mecca. Since the verse then adds, and those around her, what is meant by “Mecca” here is “the people of Mecca.” Those around her are all people across the globe, in the sense that their lands surround Mecca. It has also been interpreted as the neighboring lands of Mecca. This statement shows God’s special regard and attention for Umm al-Qurá, which is the holy sanctuary where the religious call was first made and whence it spread.

There are two possibilities for the conjunction “and” in and that you may warn the Mother of Cities: (1) it adds to blessed; (2) it adds to verifying. Some exegetes have favored the first possibility, where the meaning

would be: “We have revealed it that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around her.” However, the second possibility is more likely because the Qur’an’s verification of the previous scriptures was also one of the purposes of its revelation.1 Then the implied meaning, as stated by al-Zamakhsharī, would be: “We have revealed this Book so that it may verify that which was before it, and that you may warn the Mother of Cities.” This possibility is further strengthened if the word is recited as li-yundhira in third person (lit. “that it may warn…”).2

1 Thus muṣaddiq (verifying) should be joined with li-tundhira, where the letter lām (that, so that, in order to; indicating purpose, ghāyah) would also apply to muṣaddiq. (Trans.)

2 The difference between the two views is where verifying would stand: in the first case it is bundled with blessed; in the second case it is joined with that you may warn. In the first case the meaning would be: “We have revealed a blessed and verifying book so that you may warn…” In the second case the … and those who believe in the hereafter believe in it…: This sentence is like a conclusion that is made from the qualities of the Book which God described above. That is: “Since this is a blessed Book which We have revealed—which verifies that which was before it, and which is sent in order to warn the people of the earth—the believers in the hereafter believe in it, for indeed it calls to eternal security and cautions them against everlasting chastisement.”

God then identifies who these believers in the hereafter are by stating a quality that is exclusive to them: and they keep a guard on their prayers. The prayer is their worship in which they remember their Lord. We see the same quality twice in Sūrah al-Muʾminūn, at the beginning and end of the list of qualities mentioned for the believers: Who are humble in their prayer (23:2) and: And those who keep a guard on their prayers (23:9). The connection between these verses suggests that “keeping a guard on prayer” means “being humble in prayer,” which refers to an inner state of subservience and meekness before God’s magnificence as one stands in a position of servitude. A more common interpretation, however, is that “keeping a guard on prayer” refers to being attentive of prayer times. Discussion on the Meaning of “Blessedness” (Barakah) in the Qur’an

Al-Rāghib says in al-Mufradāt:

The root meaning of bark means “camel’s chest” although the root is also used in other meanings. “This camel has birkah” means that it has a wide chest. Baraka al-baʿīr means that the camel sat on its knees [whereby its chest is placed on the ground]. An implication of this [sitting of the camel] is that it becomes stable, fixed and settled. This implication is what is sometimes meant when the root is used. For example it is said: ibtarikū fīal-ḥarb, meaning “stay at and adhere to your position in the battle.” The place in the battlefield where warriors stay at is called barākāʾ and barūkāʾ al-ḥarb. Ibtarakat al-dābbah means that the animal stopped [and thus became fixed and settled]. Burūk means the same. Birkah (pond, pool, reservoir) is a place that holds water.

Barakah (blessing) means “sustained and fixed good that God meaning would be: “We have revealed a blessed book so that it may verify and so that you (or it) may warn…” (Trans.)

places in something.” God says: We would certainly have opened up for them blessings (barakāt) from the heaven and the earth

(7:96). These blessings are called barakāt (plural of barakah)

because of the aspect of fixedness and stability of good in them, just like the fixedness and stability of water in a pond (birkah). Mubārak (blessed) means “that in which good is established.”

This is what is meant in the verse: And this is a blessed (mubārak) reminder which We have revealed (21:50)… Now, God’s good is rooted in the unseen, cannot be measured, and is unlimited. Therefore, [even though barakah primarily means divine good,] sometimes mubārak and barakah are used for any non-physical abundance. This sense [of immaterial abundance] is what is meant in the narration, “No charity reduces

from wealth.” Upon hearing this, a loser said: “Let the scale judge between us!” However, the narration does not refer to apparent and visible reduction.…

God is called tabāraka (blessed), which refers to the exclusivity of all good to Him.

Given the above, the reality of barakah is “established good in something.” Here are some examples of this: (1) Having barakah in progeny

means having abundant descendants, or having one’s [good] name remain through one’s descendants. (2) Having barakah in food means feeding a large number of people to satiation. (3) Having barakah in time means being able to perform a task in a timespan that it is not typically doable in. Meanwhile, in the context of religion, goals and objectives are strictly restricted to either spiritual happiness or worldly achievements that result in eternal happiness in the hereafter [as opposed to transient material endowments]. Therefore, the barakah (blessing) of material things is the spiritual good that is either found directly in them, or that ensues from them. For example, when the angels descended upon Abraham they told him: The mercy of Allah and His blessings are on you, O people of the house

(11:73), where God’s “blessings” (barakāt) can refer to a variety of spiritual goods such as religion and divine proximity, as well as worldly goods such as wealth, extensive progeny, and persistence of one’s remembrance—all of which would again reduce to spiritual goods.

If something has barakah, it means that it fulfills the benefit that is desired from it and brings about the good that is sought in it. This makes barakah relative: it differs according to one’s objective and expectation of things. For example, there are several possible objectives that can be expected from food, such as: (1) to satiate hunger; (2) to not harm the eater; (3) to cure someone or make the person healthy; (4) to become spiritual light in the soul and help the person serve God. The barakah of food in each case would be the establishment of the respective good in it. This can occur if God gathers the different causes and factors of that good congruously and removes its impediments.

This should clarify that when God gives barakah to something and establishes good in it, it does not cancel the rest of causes and factors that affect it. As we have repeatedly said before, when God wills a quality or condition in something, it does not annul the entire system of causes and effects which govern that thing. That would be the case if God’s will (irādah) stands in a parallel or horizontal (ʿarḍī) position compared to the other means and causes. But that is not true. Instead, God’s will has a vertical or longitudinal (ṭūlī) relationship with other means and causes.1 For example, when God sends barakah upon food, it means that He aligns the different relevant factors in such a way that the person does not suffer any harm from eating that food. Similarly, His barakah in wealth is that He sets the different factors in line with each other, such that the wealth is not wasted, lost, stolen, plundered and so on. It does not mean that He annuls the rest of the means and causes, and instead takes charge of creating the desired good in that thing without the involvement of any intermediaries. The reader should reflect on this.

The concept of barakah (blessing) has been repeatedly used in various forms in several verses of the Holy Qur’an, as it has also been used

frequently in hadith. Similarly, we see this term used frequently in the two Testaments, where God blesses certain prophets, or some priests bless certain individuals. In fact, giving barakah is an ongoing custom in the Old Testament.

The above should clarify the error of those who deny the truth behind

(6:93) And who is more unjust than he who forges a lie against Allah, or says: It has been revealed to me; while nothing has been revealed to him, and he who says: I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed? And if you had seen when the unjust shall be in the agonies of death and the angels stretching out their hands: Give up your souls; today shall you be recompensed with an ignominious chastisement because you spoke against Allah other than the truth and (because) you showed pride toward His communications.

This verse lists three forms of wrongdoing that rank highest in terms of injustice. No sound intellect would doubt their enormity and abomination, and that is why they are presented in form of a rhetorical question.

The verse effectively invites the audience to settle with the rule of sound intellect, be fair, and submit to explicit truth. It says to the Prophet: “Tell them that both I and you should not defy the truth and should not transgress against God by committing the greatest and most heinous injustice, which is injustice with regards to God. So how can you forge a lie against God by claiming that He has associates and referring to them for intercession? And how could I make claims to prophethood and say that ‘it has been revealed to me’ if I were not truly a prophet to whom God has revealed? And how can someone say that ‘I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed,’ when—in doing so—he derides God’s rules and mocks His communications?”

The result of these instructions is that the audience would end up accepting prophethood [of the Prophet Muḥammad]. If they stop forging the false claim of polytheism against God; if one does not vainly claim that I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed; and if the Prophet continues his claim to revelation, then what remains would be his claim without any challenge.

“Forging a lie against God” includes the claim that “it has been revealed to me” while it has not. Therefore it has been said that the second injustice mentioned in the verse is a particular example of the first, which is mentioned separately to show the significance and high status of the subject

of revelation. However, if we contemplate the context of the verse and the fact that it is directed at the polytheists, it can be inferred that “forging a lie

against God” primarily refers to “assuming partners for God.” The whole message of the verse is to encourage fairness and put down the bigotry of the pre-Islamic era (jāhiliyyah). Therefore, it does not make sense for the second injustice mentioned in the verse to be a particular example of the first [because that would itself be an unfair way of expression]. The verse only makes a vague and overall reference to its intended meaning without explicitly specifying it in order to not stimulate any bigotry and fanaticism in the audience.

In short, the first and second forms of injustice mentioned in the verse—he who forges a lie against Allah and or says: It has been revealed to me; while nothing has been revealed to him—differ in terms of their intent, even though it appears that one is a particular example of another. This interpretation is confirmed by what comes next, which threatens the audience with punishment and asks them about their partners and intercessors

[that they had assumed besides God, as we shall see in the next verse]. Some exegetes have said that the second form of injustice—or says: It has been revealed to me; while nothing has been revealed to him— was revealed in reference to Musaylimah who claimed to be a prophet. However, this does not match the theme of the verse, as we explained above. Rather, this form of injustice apparently refers to the Prophet himself. Of course, the verse still retains its general meaning which is applicable to anyone if we take it by itself and irrespective of its specific context.

We should also add that this chapter is Meccan, while Musaylimah’s claim to prophethood occurred after the Prophet’s migration to Medina. Those who have offered the above interpretation believe that this verse was revealed in Medina, not Mecca. We shall discuss this view under our following examination of narrations, by God’s will.

… and he who says: I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed?...: This part of the verse apparently recounts a statement that was actually made at the time. That is, there was someone who claimed that “I shall reveal something similar to what God has revealed.” This expression makes mock of the Qur’an as “what God has revealed” because the person claims that “I can also reveal the like of it.” Otherwise, [if his claim were concerning the content of the Qur’an,] he should have said: “I will say the

like of what Muḥammad has said” or “I will bring to you the like of what he has brought to you.”

Some exegetes have said that this claim refers to what is narrated elsewhere from the polytheists: If we wished we could say the like of it; this is

nothing but the fables of the ancients (8:31).

Others have said that the verse was revealed in Medina about ʿAbdAllāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ, who said, “I reveal the like of what God reveals.” Other suggestions have also been made which we shall discuss in our examination of narrations, by God’s will. Overall, apparently the verse does not match any of these views. The structure of the claim mentioned in the verse shows that it is a promise concerning the future, while the claim if we wished… (8:31) is a conditional statement, and ʿAbd-Allāh’s claim—assuming that its narration is authentic—refers to something in the present.

Either way, this third form of injustice—and he who says: I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed—relates a claim that some Arab polytheist made in defiance of God’s revelation. It should be noted that the Arabic

particle man (he who) is repeated for the third type of injustice, but not the second type: he who (man) forges a lie…or says…and he who (man) says: I will reveal…. Based on this point, the three forms of injustice in the verse can be classified under two categories: in the first two types, the person admits and submits to God and His revelation as an overall idea, but in the third type he equates himself with God and denies the truth of divine revelation altogether.

… And if you had seen when the unjust shall be in the agonies (ghamarāt) of death and the angels stretching out their hands (bāsiṭū aydīhim): Give up your souls; today shall you be recompensed with an ignominious (al-hūn) chastisement because you spoke against Allah other than

the truth and (because) you showed pride toward His communications: The root meaning of ghamr is “to cover something and not leave any trace of it.” Thus ghamrah is used in the following meanings: (1) a great amount of water that covers what is underneath it; (2) total ignorance; and (3) a difficulty that envelops someone. Ghamarāt means shadāʾid (difficulties, intensities, adversities), as used in this verse: shall be in the agonies

(ghamarāt) of death(6:93). Hūn and hawān mean dhillah (humiliation, dishonor, abasement).

The literal meaning of basṭ al-yad is clear [that is: opening, extending or spreading one’s hand], but it is often used metaphorically, where its

meaning differs according to context. For instance, when it is said that a rich person “stretches out his hand,” it refers to his generosity and financial aid toward the needy. If a king “has an open hand,” it means that he can govern the affairs of his nation without any conflict or opposition. If a rough and tough agent “extends his hand” toward a culprit who is arrested, it refers to the agent beating and dragging the culprit.

Therefore, the angels stretching out their hands refers to the angels starting to punish the wrongdoers. The flow of the verse suggests that the next

part of the verse explains what the angels will do with these wrongdoers: Give up your souls; today shall you be recompensed with an ignominious chastisement…. In other words, these are the words of the angels, not the words of God. The implied meaning is: “The angels will tell them: Give up your souls….” This means that the angels will capture their souls in a painful way that makes them taste an intense punishment. This is their punishment upon death, when they move from this world to the realm that is beyond. Then they shall have another punishment later upon the Resurrection, as God says elsewhere: and before them is a barrier until the day they are raised (23:100).

Given the above, “today” in today shall you be recompensed means “the day of their death”—or in other words, the barzakh (the intermediate realm between this life and the Resurrection). That is when they will

be given the chastisement mentioned in the verse. It should also be clear that “the unjust” refers to those who have committed one of the three greatest forms of injustice that God counted in the first part of the verse: (1) forging a lie against God; (2) falsely claiming to be a prophet; and (3) mocking God’s revelation. These three forms of injustice closely tie into the next part of the verse, which explains two reasons for their chastisement. The first reason is: because you spoke against Allah other than the truth. This refers to one who forges a lie against God by attributing a partner to Him, or by falsely ascribing a legal rule or revelation to Him. The second reason is: and (because) you showed pride toward His communications. This refers to one who says: I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed. It also follows that give up your souls is an existential or creational command (al-amr al-takwīnī),1 because death and giving up one’s soul is not something in one’s control so that the person may be ordered [legislatively and authoritatively] to do it. The same is true about life, as the

Qur’an says: It is He W ho causes death and gives life (53:44). Therefore, the command in this verse is an existential one, and the angels are the means and agents that implement it. The command to give up your souls is meant figuratively as is a metaphorical image: It is as though the human soul is something inside the body through which the body lives; and if it leaves the body, the person will die. This view is according to God’s Book, which clearly suggests that the soul is not of the same nature as the body, meaning that it is not physical or material. It is a different form of being, but is

united with and attached to the body through some immaterial form of union and attachment. We discussed this in the first volume of this book,2 and we shall discuss it further under other relevant verses, by God’s will. Overall, give up your souls refers to the detachment of their souls from their bodies, which marks their death. The context suggests that this is part of the angels’ speech [not God’s].

The meaning is: “I wish you could see the time when these wrongdoers shall experience the pangs and agonies of death, when the angels will

start to chastise them by seizing their spirits firmly and informing them that they shall enter the realm of death, where they will be punished with humiliation and dishonor as their retribution for speaking against God other than the truth and showing pride toward His communications.”
