(6:94) And certainly you have come to Us alone (furādá) as We created you at first, and you have lefiibehind your backs the things which We gave you (khawwalnākum, from takhwīl), and We do not see with you your intercessors about whom you asserted that they were (Allah’s) associates in respect to you; certainly the ties between you are now cut offand what you asserted is gone from you.

Furādá is the plural of fard (individual, alone, single), which means “someone or something that is detached from mixing with others in some aspect.” Its opposite is zawj (pair, couple, joined), which means “someone or something that is mixed with others.” The two are respectively similar in meaning to witr (odd, solo) and shafʿ (even), because witr is “that which is not attached to something else,” while shafʿ is “that which is attached to something else.” Takhwīl means “to give someone possession, authority and control over some wealth or the like.”

W hat is meant by “intercessors” in this verse is the lords that they used to worship besides God in order to intercede for them before God. They assumed them to be God’s partners in His creation so that they may intercede for them. This verse talks about the reality of human life, which will become evident to them when they return to their Lord by death. At that point they will behold the reality of themselves: that their life and all their affairs have ever been subject to God’s direction alone, just as they were when they were first created. They adopted partners for God in order to intercede for them; they spent their life trying to secure various means and connections for themselves; and they endeavored to back and strengthen themselves by their wealth, children, spouses, relatives and communities. However, at that point they will realize that all these things which they used to seek were futile thoughts and false illusions without any impact in the realm of creation whatsoever.

Humankind is a part of the universe like any other part: they are all under God’s direction, moving toward the end that God has set for them. Nothing has any influence or say in God’s direction and facilitation of affairs except as a means or factor whose impact traces back to Him, without the thing having any independent impact of its own.

The thing is that once human beings are created and come to existence, they see the adornment of this world, take note of the apparent

means and intercessors that seem to be at work, and are attracted to the pleasures of life. Thus their souls become attached to these pleasures, and in order to reach these pleasures, they chase after the apparent means of this life and become subservient to them. This distracts them from turning their attention to the Creator and Facilitator of these means, W ho is

the Cause of the causes and the Director of all affairs. As a result, they deem these apparent means to be independent in their impact, and their only concern and objective becomes achieving the pleasures of this material life by submitting to the apparent system of means and instruments

which seems to govern this world. This is how their entire life in this world is spent playing and sporting with these illusions and imaginations, all because of their carnal souls that are so fascinated with the glamor of the material life. Hence their life is immersed in playing with false illusions which distract them from the truth. This is what God says: And this life of the world is nothing but a sport and a play (29:64).

Based on the teachings of the Qur’an, when people take offthe robe of servitude [to God], they forget their Lord, which in turn leads them to forget themselves. The Qur’an says: those who forgot Allah, so He made them forgot their own souls: these it is that are the transgressors (59:19). When the soul leaves the body at death, the person will be disconnected from all material means, causes and instruments to which he was

linked through his body and was connected to in this life. At that point the person will see how the presumed independence, grandeur and influence of these means all fade away. There he will realize that his affair from the beginning to end was up to nobody and nothing but his Lord. He will learn that has no lord other than God, and no one else has any influence on him. Given the above explanations, the verse can be interpreted as follows: And certainly you have come to Us alone as We created you at first…: This part expresses the fact of the matter [about the creation and reality of humans].

… and you have lefiibehind your backs the things which We gave you…: This refers to the annulment of the means which engage the person from his Lord as he is busy with them from the onset of his creation until when he is captured upon death and taken to his Lord.

… certainly the ties between you are now cut offand what you asserted is gone from you: This explains why the person is severed from the means and why they cease to have any impact of their own. It is because of an unveiling for the person, whereby he will realize that the presumed means which he was busy playing with throughout his life were nothing but false illusions.

Thus it should be clear that the apparent means and accessories in human life have no share of reality other than toys that people play with, and illusions that occupy their lives.

(6:95) Surely Allah is the Splitter (fāliq, from falq) of the grain and the date-stone [to germinate]; He brings forth the living from the dead and He is the bringer forth of the dead from the living; that is Allah! How are you then turned away.

Falq is synonymous with shaqq (to split, to crack). The last verse said that the apparent means in this world are not independent in their impact, and the lords which people have taken are not intercessors so that people may worship them besides God. This verse moves on to say that these things which have preoccupied the people are nothing but creatures of God that are subject to His direction. They have no impact or action that improves human life and leads to the goal of their creation except by God’s measurement and direction. God, and only God, is the sole director of all affairs in the universe; hence there is no lord other than Him.

God is the One Who splits the grain and stones, which then grow into plants and trees that feed the people with seeds and fruits. He is the One Who brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living. We discussed what this means under verse 3:27.1 This is God and no one else! So what turns you away?! Until when will you be diverted from the truth toward falsehood?

1 See volume 5 of the English translation, pp. 197ff. (Trans.)

(6:96) Splitter of the dawn (al-iṣbāḥ); and He has made the night for rest (sakanan), and the sun and the moon for reckoning (ḥusbānan); this is an arrangement of the Mighty, the Knowing.

Iṣbāḥ here means ṣubḥ (morning, dawn), but it is originally an infinitive (to dawn, to start the morning). Sakan is “where one rests.” Ḥusbān

is the plural of ḥisāb (measurement, count, calculation). It has also been defined as an infinitive that means “to count, to calculate.” The conjunction “and” in and He has made the night for rest joins the sentence to splitter of the dawn. This is a permissible conjunction even though the first part of the verse [splitter of the dawn] has no verb unlike the second part [He has made the night for rest] because the first part effectively has a verbal meaning [that is, “He causes the dawn to break”]. The second part has also been recited as “and the Maker (jāʿil) of the night.…”1 The verse mentions a few things: (1) the splitting of the dawn; (2) making the night for rest, when animals rest from their activity to recover their lost energy and discharge the weariness, lassitude and fatigue that they have accumulated due to their daily activity; (3) making the sun and the moon a means of reckoning because we can discern nights, days, months and years based on their movements which are visible to us. These resemble an astonishing arrangement and measurement of things in a world that is constantly subject to change and movement. These signs facilitate and give order to the life of humankind. This is why the verse ends by saying: this is an arrangement of the Mighty, the Knowing. Since He is Mighty, nothing can overcome Him and ruin how He regulates the affairs. Since He is Knowledgeable, He is not ignorant of any requirement for the well-functioning of His kingdom, such that His system may fall apart and cease to continue.

(6:97) And He it is Who has made the stars for you that you might follow the right way thereby in the darkness of the land and the sea; truly We have elaborated the signs (al-āyāt) for a people who know.

1 In this case, fāliq and jāʿil in the first two parts of the verse would be consistent

because they are both nouns. The first two parts of the verse would then be both nominal sentences. (Trans.)

The meaning of the verse is clear. The elaboration of āyāt (signs, communications) can have two meanings: (1) providing detailed signs in the

realm of creation (takwīn); or (2) explaining communications in detail [where communications would be verbal signs of God].

God has two wills with respect to these enormous heavenly bodies: (1) He has ordained that they should serve the welfare of humans through the movements that they seem to have in our senses. (2) He has an independent will that governs each of them [irrespective of the human world].

These wills do not negate one another because they pertain to different aspects. The occurrence of one aspect of God’s will does not nullify the occurrence of another aspect. At the same time, all pieces of the universe are connected to one another in a uniform network.

(6:98) And He it is Who has produced you from a single soul, and (has given you) a dwelling-place (mustaqarr) and a repository (mustawdaʿ); indeed We have elaborated the signs for a people who discern.

The verse has been recited with both mustaqarr and mustaqirr.

Mustaqarr is ism makān (noun of place, locative noun), meaning “the place of rest and settlement.” In that case mustawdaʿ would also be a noun of place, meaning “the place where something is stored for a while.” These two words are also mentioned in the verse: And there is no animal in the earth but on Allah is the sustenance of it, and He knows its dwelling-place (mustaqarrahā) and its repository (mustawdaʿahā); all is in a manifest book

(11:6). Based on this recitation [of mustaqarr], the verse would involve some omission for the purpose of brevity. The implied meaning is: “Then of you some are in a dwelling-place, and some are in a repository.” If the word is recited as mustaqirr, which is semantically preferred, it would be an active participle noun as a subject, while mustawdaʿ would be a passive participle noun as an object. The implied meaning would be: “Then of you there are some who have settled, and some who have been deposited temporarily but not settled yet.”

And He it is Who has produced you (anshaʾakum, from inshāʾ) from a single soul…: Apparently what is meant here is that the human population, despite its multitude and spread, all go back to Adam, who, according

to the Qur’an, was the origin of the current generation of human beings. Mustaqirr refers to those human beings who have been born and have settled in the earth, which is the mustaqarr of humankind, as He says: and there is for you in the earth an abode (mustaqarr) (2:36). Mustawdaʿ refers to those human beings who are not born yet, but are still deposited in the loins of men and wombs of women, to be born later. This interpretation is most appropriate given the verse’s theme about how all members

of this species have come forth from a single person. It is also possible to interpret mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ as verbal nouns (sing. maṣdar).1 The verse uses inshāʾ (to produce, to originate) as opposed to khalq (to create) and other similar terms, because inshāʾ suggests a sudden origination as opposed to a gradual one.2

Note: the interpretation that we offered here [for mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ] also fits another verse where both words have appeared, which we already quoted: And there is no animal in the earth but on Allah is the sustenance of it, and He knows its dwelling-place (mustaqarrahā) and its repository (mustawdaʿahā)(11:6). It means: “He knows those which have settled in the earth by being already created, and He also knows those that are not yet created and have not settled in the earth but are on the way to being created.”

The meaning of the current verse [6:98] is: “And He is the One Who brought you into being, O community of humankind, all from a single soul. He made you build the land until an appointed time. Thus the land is always occupied by you as long as your species is not extinct. At any given time, some of you are dwelling in the land, and some of you are deposited in the loins of men and the wombs of women, or only the loins of men, heading to dwell in the land later.”

Here is a list of other interpretations suggested by the exegetes: “Being produced from a single soul” means that everyone has the same

1 In this case mustaqarr would mean the act of “dwelling or settlement”; and mustawdaʿ would mean the act of “deposition or entrustment.” The meaning would be: “Then there is settlement [for some] and there is reposition [for others].” In cases like this, verbal nouns can also have either the subjective or

objective meaning. The meaning would be: “Some of you are to settle—or to be settled—and some of you are to be deposited for now.” (Trans.)

2 Inshāʾ is creation that is followed by growing and fostering, but it is not preceded by any previous example or stage. (Trans.)

kind of soul, which is the human soul.

It means that everyone is of the same species, which is a combination of soul and body. This is the reality of the human being, which consists of a human soul and a human body.

Mustaqarr means the wombs, and mustawdaʿ means the loins.

Mustaqarr means the earth, and mustawdaʿ means the graves.

Mustaqarr means the wombs, and mustawdaʿ means the earth or the graves.

Mustaqarr means the spirit, and mustawdaʿ means the body.

There are more interpretations to add to this list, but there is not much benefit in discussing them.

(6:99) And He it is Who sends down water from above (al-samāʾ), then We bring forth with it plants of every kind, then We bring forth from it green (foliage) (khaḍiran) from which We produce grain piled up (mutarākiban) (in the ear); and of the palm-tree, of the sheaths of it (ṭalʿihā), come forth clusters (qinwān) (of dates) within reach (dāniyah), and gardens of grapes and olives and pomegranates, alike and unlike; behold the fruit of it when it yields the fruit and the ripening of it (yanʿihi);

most surely there are signs in this for a people who believe.

Samāʾ here means “up, above.” Anything that is above someone and shades the person is samāʾ [for that person]. Khaḍir means akhḍar (green, as in the color). It is apparently a contraction of khāḍir (greens, as vegetables). When grains are laid one on top of another they are called mutarākib, as in an ear. Ṭalʿ is the first part of a palm’s fruit that appears. Qinwān is the plural of qinw, which means ʿidhq, which is a cluster of dates just like ʿunqūd (a bunch of grapes). Dāniyah is synonymous with qarībah (close, near). Alike and unlike means fruits that are similar and dissimilar in terms of kind, shape and other properties. Yanʿ means “the ripening of a fruit.”

… then We bring forth with it plants (nabāt) of every kind…:Nabāt (plant, vegetation) here has been interpreted as the blossoming and growth that is found in anything with vegetative power. The meaning would be: “By means of the water which We send down from above, We make this hidden faculty manifest.” In other words, “Through rain We grow anything that grows, including plants, trees, humans and other animals.”

In these verses [6:95-99], God lists certain parts of His creation for those possessed of sight and insight to see and reflect upon, so that they may be guided to His oneness. These can be classified into a few categories: Things that have to do with the earth, such as splitting the grain and stones [6:95];

Things that have to do with the heaven, such as the night, the day, the sun, the moon and the stars [6:96-97];

Things that have to do with humankind, such as creating their species from a single soul, and their members having already settled [in the

earth] or else deposited there [for the time being] [6:98];

Things that have to do with all of the above, such as sending rain from above, thereby producing food in the form of plants, grains and fruits, and growing things that have a vegetative faculty such as plants, animals and humans [6:99].

Stars are specifically described as a sign for a people who know (6:97); the production of human souls is specifically described as a sign for a people who discern (6:98); and the system of vegetation is specifically described as a sign for a people who believe (6:99). The connection should be clear: the system of vegetation in the universe is something clear and simple. One only needs to look at it in order to understand it, without any further effort. The only condition is that person’s gaze must be illuminated by the fairness of faith, not defiled by the impurity of defiance

and stubbornness. As with observing the stars and heavenly events, it is not something that an ordinary mind can comprehend without effort. It is rather the people of knowledge who appreciate it and understand the position of the stars and what happens in the heavens. Finally, coming to know the human souls and the secrets of their creation is something that requires not only theoretical knowledge and mental learning, but also inward consciousness, intense contemplation and arduous perseverance—which amount to fiqh (discernment, deep understanding).

(6:100) And they make (jaʿalū, from jaʿl) the jinn associates with Allah, while (wa) He created them, and they falsely attribute to Him sons and daughters without knowledge; glory be to Him, and highly exalted is He above what they ascribe (to Him).

The verb jaʿl (make, assign) can have either one or two objects. In the first case, its object would be associates, and the jinn would be interpretive of that. In the second case, the jinn would be the first object and associates would be the second.1 Apparently the particle wa (and, but, while) here means “while.” Some grammarians have not permitted such a usage, but their argument is not clear. At any rate the statement while He created them (or and He created them) is meant to refute the polytheists. The meaning is: “They have ascribed the jinn as partners to God while He is the One Who has created the jinn.” It is not possible for the created to be a partner of its Creator and at His level.

The jinn here would be “the devils.” An example of their association with God would be the dualistic belief in Yazdān (the good principle) and Ahriman (the evil principle) that is attributed to the Majūs (Magians, Zoroastrians). Another example would be Yazīdiyyah, who believed in Satan (Iblīs) as a deity (which they call Peacock Angel and consider to be the king of all angels). The jinn may also refer to the well-known creatures [in Qur’anic terminology]. This would match a belief that is attributed to the polytheists: that God married a jinn lady, and from them angels were born. This possibility flows better with the next part of the verse: And they make the jinn associates with Allah, while He created them, and they falsely attribute (kharaqū) to Him sons and daughters without knowledge (6:100). Given this interpretation, sons and daughters would both be angels. They have “cut” (kharaqū) these angels for Him, meaning that they have falsely come up with them and attributed them to God. Glory be to Him, and highly exalted is He above what they ascribe (to Him).

If sons and daughters are more inclusive than the angels, then they would refer to what people of other religions held. For example, Hindus

1 The current translation is based on the second case. In the first case the meaning would be: “And they ascribe associates to Allah, the jinn,” where the order better matches the order of words in the Arabic text of the verse. (Trans.)

and Buddhists have beliefs similar to those of Christians who believe that the Christ is God’s son. Similarly, archaeological discoveries show that other ancient idolaters believed in sons and daughters for God, whom they used to worship. The Arab polytheists also believed that the angels are God’s daughters. We discussed these views under verses 3:79-80.1

(6:101) Originator (badīʿ) of the heavens and the earth! How could He have a son when He has no consort, and He (Himself) created everything, and He is the Knower of all things.

This verse is a response to the polytheists’ belief in God having sons and daughters [mentioned in the last verse]. The verse provides two arguments in negation of this view: (1) The only way for God to have a real

child is to have a spouse; given that He has no spouse, how can He have a child? (2) He is the Creator and Originator of everything, but a child is part of the parents which grows [into another independent being] through fertilization. Clearly a part of something cannot be created by it. These two arguments are summed up in the fact that He is the original Creator of the heavens and the earth, where nothing in the universe is similar to Him in any aspect.2 Thus, how can He have a spouse that He has married or children that are of the same kind as Him? We are informed of this by God Who is completely free from ignorance: He is the Knower of all things. Referring to our discussion under verse 3:79 (It is not meet for a mortal that Allah should give him…) would be helpful here.3

1 See volume 6 (1st ed.) of the English translation, pp. 132ff. (Trans.)

2 This shows that the author has implicitly interpreted badīʿ (Originator) as “a Creator who is Himself unique and without any like.” The more apparent and common meaning of badīʿ is “a Creator whose creation is unique and unprecedented.” (Trans.)

(6:102) That is Allah, your Lord, there is no god but He; the Creator of all things, therefore serve Him, and He is Guardian over all things. This verse is a conclusion that is made following the previous verses. It means: “Since the matter is as We said above, your Lord is Allah Whom We described for you, not anyone else.”

… there is no god but He…: This is an explicit statement of God’s unity which was implicit in the first part of the verse. At the same time it explains and justifies the previous statement. That is: “He is the Lord and there is no other lord besides Him because He is God and there is no god besides Him. After all, can someone be a lord (rabb) without being a god (ilāh)?” … the Creator of all things…: This sentence explains and justifies the last sentence, that there is no god but He. That is: “There is no other god but Him because He is the Creator of everything without any exception.” Since there is no other creator of anything, nothing can be His partner in being a god who deserves to be served. Since all things are His creatures, they are all subservient servants and worshipers of Him [existentially], which means that they are not His equals and associates in being worshiped. … therefore serve Him…: This is stated as a conclusion of that is Allah, your Lord. It means: “Since no one else is your Lord but God, you must serve Him.”

… and He is Guardian over all things: That is: “He is the One Who watches over everything, directs its affairs, and organizes its existence and life.” Given this, one must fear Him and not associate partners with Him out of ignorance. Therefore, this sentence effectively emphasizes therefore serve Him. In other words, “Do not disdain to serve Him because He is a guardian over you, and He is not heedless of your actions.”

(6:103) No vision comprehends Him, but He comprehends all vision;

and He is the All-Subtle, the All-Aware.

The last verse was addressed to the polytheists, whose simple understanding would interpret He is Guardian over all things (6:102) in a physical

sense. They would assume God to be a physical being like other physical beings that act in the corporeal world. Hence this verse addresses and refutes such a misconception by saying: No vision comprehends Him. He is not comprehended by the eyes because He is transcendent of physicality and its properties.

… but He comprehends all vision…: This clarifies another misconception that would spring to the minds of the polytheists because of

being accustomed to thinking about everything materially, and because of being immersed in their five senses and physical objects. They would assume that if the eyes do not comprehend God, then He is detached from the senses and physical objects, without any existential connection with them to know and observe them. As a result, He must be severed from His creatures: He cannot know them just as they do not know Him, and He cannot see anything just as nothing sees Him. God clarifies this misunderstanding by saying: but He comprehends all vision.

… and He is the All-Subtle (al-laṭīf), the All-Aware (al-khabīr): This justifies the previous claim. Laṭīfimeans “something fine that penetrates something else.” Khabīr is derived from khubrah (expertise, awareness, cognizance). Since God encompasses all things in the real sense of it, He witnesses everything; neither the outward nor the inward aspect of anything escapes from Him.1 At the same time He possesses knowledge and awareness, meaning that He knows the outward and inward aspect of everything without anything engaging Him or veiling Him from another. Thus He comprehends both the faculty of sight and what the faculty sees, as opposed to ordinary vision which only beholds the seen.

Instead of saying that God comprehends the people who have sight, it says that He comprehends the sights. This is because God’s comprehension is different from our sensory perceptions which comprehend the

outward aspects of things, which are accidental to them.2 Our sight, for example, comprehends light, color, farness, nearness, largeness, smallness, movement and stillness. For God, however, the accidents as well as the substances that carry them are fully present, both outwardly and inwardly. They are all patent to Him without being veiled or absent from Him in any way. Thus He comprehends the total reality of sight, while no sight can comprehend Him.

These two verses [6:102-103] are fascinating in terms of their brilliant

1 This is the author’s interpretation of al-laṭīf (the All-Subtle); an implication of

this quality is that God encompasses everything both outwardly and inwardly. (Trans.)

2 Here, “accident” (ʿaraḍī) is employed in its logical sense, meaning a property of a thing that is not essential to its nature, as opposed to “substance” (jawhar).

expression, easy flow, and brevity. They also lead one who reflects upon them to hidden mysteries.

Discussion on the Universality of Creation and its Inclusion of Everything

That is Allah, your Lord, there is no god but He; the Creator of all things: The apparent meaning of this sentence is the universality of creation, meaning that anything with any share of existence and reality has been created and brought to existence by God. God’s description as the Creator of all things has also appeared in other places in His Book, and nowhere is there any evidence to restrict or limit its universality in any way whatsoever. The other verses are: Say: Allah is the Creator of all things, and He

is the One, the Dominant (13:16); Allah is the Creator of all things and He is a Guardian over everything (39:62); That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things; there is no God but He (40:62).

This topic has kindled astonishing quarrels among the followers of different sects and schools, leading to a variety of views on the subject. This is not something exclusively limited to Muslim theologians and philosophers, but has also been a subject of hot debate among Jewish and

Christian thinkers. We are not concerned with presenting the views and arguments of the scholars here, because this is an exegesis of the Qur’an. Our job here is to infer the Qur’an’s view on the topic based on other relevant verses.1

When we look at the things which exist in the universe—such as the sky, the planets, the stars, the earth, the mountains, the lowlands, the fields, the oceans, the deserts, the elements, the minerals, the clouds, the thunder, the lightning, the thunderbolt, the rain, the hail, the plants, the trees, the animals and the humans—we find them to have certain properties and effects which they cause and create, and which can be attributed to these beings as an action is attributed to its actor, or an effect to its cause. The Qur’an verifies this view and ascription.

It also confirms that humans have certain actions that are attributable to them like any other being, such as eating, drinking, walking, sitting,

1 The main controversy here is about “the createdness of actions,” especially human actions. That is: “Are the actions of human beings created and caused by humans or by God?” As the author explains both ascriptions are true in a sense based on the Qur’an. (Trans.)

growing, understanding, realizing, rejoicing, delighting, being healthy and falling ill. The Qur’an does not make any difference between the human being and the other species in this sense. It talks about the different actions of human beings and gives them commands and prohibitions. None of these would make sense if humans did not have actions that are attributable to them. This means that the Qur’an views human beings just as we

view them in our societies: we believe them to have certain actions and effects that are attributable to them; we hold them accountable for some of their actions which go back to their choice and volition in one way or another, such as eating, drinking, and walking; and we overlook some of their other properties that are not based on their free will, such as health, illness, youth, and age.

Therefore, the Qur’an’s view of the system at work in the universe matches our primary understanding of the world it based on our sensory observations and rational experience. It is a system of beings of different kinds and natures, each of which has certain functions, has certain

impacted on other beings, and is also affected by them. This is how the entire universe is arranged, where each part of it is completely related to all other parts. This is the universal law of causality which governs all contingent beings. According to this law, whenever we have something that may or may not exist [in and of itself], it should be given existence by another being [that is, it should be existentiated externally, from an outside source]. If the cause of something is absent, then the existence of that thing—the effect—is impossible. The Qur’an confirms this law and its universal application. Had this not been true or not universally applicable, one could not argue by it at all in any capacity. This is while the Qur’an has argued by it to prove the existence of the Creator and His qualities of oneness, power, knowledge, and so on.

Just as it is impossible for an effect to exist without its cause, it is also necessary for it to exist given its cause—because of the necessary existential relation between the two. God has approved this by using it in many

places in His Book, where He states His noble attributes in order to prove their effects, consequences and implications. For example He says: and He is the One, the Dominant (13:16); Surely Allah is Mighty, Avenger (14:47); Then surely Allah is Mighty, Wise (2:209); Surely Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

(2:173). He has also established many events and matters by referring to their consequences and implications that have occurred afterwards. For example He says: But they would not believe in what they had rejected before

(10:74). Likewise, there are many other verses which talk about the believers, the disbelievers and the hypocrites. If it were possible for an effect

to deviate from and fail its cause—assuming that the required conditions of its occurrence are met and its impediments are absent—then certainly none of these arguments would hold.

Hence, the Qur’an accepts that the world of existence is governed by the universal law of causality. It confirms that there is one or many causes for any being or accident that exists and for any event that occurs, such that if the cause is there then the effect must necessarily exist, and if the cause is not there then the effect cannot exist. This is the first observation that can be made when contemplating the Qur’an [in this regard].

Then, upon further study, we notice that God extends His creation to anything in the universe which can be called a “thing” (shayʾ). He says: Say: Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Dominant (13:16), as well as the other verses in this regard which we quoted above [6:102, 39:62, 40:62]. This is based on the fact that His causality (ʿilliyyah) and agency (fāʿiliyyah) encompass all things despite the causal relationships that exist among the [contingent] beings at their own level—which we discussed above.1 For example the Qur’an says: He, Whose is the kingdom of the heavens and the earth…and Who created everything, then ordained for it a measure (25:2); He Who gave to everything its creation, then guided it (to its goal) (20:50); Who created and shaped, and Who measured and guided (87:2-3).

We see another expression in these verses, where things are described as being created. Their actions, effects, movements and states are attributed to God’s measurement and guidance. This means that the specific

actions and properties of things trace to God’s decree and measurement. One example is the movement of human beings who walk from one place to another, the fish which swim in the sea, and the birds which fly with their wings, as He says: of them [the living creatures] is that which walks upon its belly, and of them is that which walks upon two feet, and of them is that which walks upon four; Allah creates what He wills (24:45). There

1 In other words, God’s action is the only, absolute and ultimate cause of every existential event in the universe. Other forces and factors that create existential

events are in fact the means and manifestations of His causality and creation. “We are all puppets in His hands; and this is the monotheistic view.” (Trans.) are numerous verses to this effect. According to these verses, the specific actions of all beings are defined and measured by God. Similarly, the goals and ends that the beings seek—despite their differences, disagreement and variety— are set for them by God’s measurement, and they move toward them by God’s guidance which accompanies them from the onset of their creation until their end. All of these go back to the arrangement of the Mighty, the Knowing (6:96).

Therefore, we can distinguish two aspects in things: (1) their [unchanging] substance and essence; and (2) their existential limits as well as the

transformations, stages and goals that they experience throughout their period of life or existence. The first aspect is attributable to God’s creation (khalq, khilqah), and the second aspect goes back to God’s measurement (taqdīr), which can be matched with the specifications of God’s creation. Yet, there are another set of verses saying that the different parts of universe are connected to one another, harmonious with each other, and

united together in existence. They are all governed by a single system that has no director other than God. This is sometimes referred to as “the argument of uniformity of direction” (burhān ittiṣāl al-tadbīr).

The above is what we can deduce by contemplating the Book of God.

However, there remain three further points that one should take note of when studying and contemplating this subject:

(1) Ascription of Sins to God

According to some scholars, there are certain things that are undoubtedly evil and abhorrent, such as various forms of wrong and injustice. The

intellect would never attribute them to God’s Holy Precinct. Likewise, the Noble Qur’an has declared God to be clear and free from every kind of wrong and injustice in several verses, such as: And your Lord is not in the least unjust to the servants (41:46); Say: Surely Allah does not enjoin indecency (7:28). This contradicts the idea that everything has been created by

God. Thus, the idea of universality of creation is subject to this exception which is backed by both rational and transmitted evidence. This means that human actions are created by human beings, but everything else beyond that is created by God, including the essence and effects of things. These scholars have further added that if human actions are created by God, then it means that they are beyond human volition, which

contradicts God’s entire system of command, prohibition, obedience, disobedience, reward, punishment, sending messengers, revealing scriptures, and enacting divine laws.

However, these scholars have missed a fine distinction between real matters [which exist as external entities] versus conventional matters [which are our mental constructions]. The latter are things that have no external existence, but they are things that human beings need to conceive (taṣawwur) or confirm (taṣdīq) in order to have a comfortable and

functional social life. This means a confusion between existential and nonexistential aspects of things. We addressed this subject in our discussion

of jabr (compulsion, determinism, predestination) and tafwīḍ (delegation, entrustment) under verses 2:26-27.1

W hat can be said in this regard is that the Qur’an apparently implies the universality of God’s creation where it says: Allah is the Creator of all things (kulli shayʾ) (6:102, 13:16, 39:62, 40:62). However, the Qur’an also says: He Who made good everything (kulla shayʾ) that He has created (32:7), which states that everything that God has created is good and beautiful. The two verses together express two points: (1) anything other than God which can be called a “thing” (shayʾ) is created by Him; and (2) anything that is created by Him is good. Therefore, “creation” and “goodness” are concomitant in existence, meaning that everything is good in the sense that it is a creation of God. In other words, the real and existential aspect of everything [which is what is attributable to God as His creation] is good and fair. The evil aspects of things are always accidental to their essence, not intrinsic. Things are evil only in a relative sense, in relation to other things, but not in their essence and reality, which is attributable to God. It is true that the Qur’an talks about sin, injustice, evil and other similar terms [as apparently and existential realities]. However, building on what we said above, we should say that these are not real concepts and titles. They are not part of the existential properties of things which can be attributed to God and described as His creation. These concepts and descriptions [of evil and sin] rather apply to things with certain actions and effects in terms of some conventional, relational or proportional aspect [not in terms of their existential aspect in reality]. Indeed,

for every disobedience and injustice there is some similar act that is not disobedience. The difference between the two is that one of them goes

For example consider adultery versus marriage: they are two similar acts that do not differ from one another in terms of their external reality and existence. Their only difference is in terms of their conformity and non-conformity with divine law, social customs, and/or collective interest. All of these are conventional and relational matters which apply to things based on how they conform to social welfare. Then they are used in turn as a basis for praise, rebuke, reward and punishment. Such relative aspects and conventional labels are only derived and determined mentally, by practical wisdom and collective human reason. They are only applicable in the realm of social conventions, but they have nothing to do with creation to begin with, except for some existential consequences that are tied to them such as reward and punishment. Creation (khilqah) and existentiation (ījād), on the other hand, pertain to the external world of existence and reality [as opposed to mental derivations and conventional classifications].

Consider an act that is viewed as injustice. It is only at the plane of convention that this act is called injustice, is considered to be evil, is viewed

as a sin, and is followed by rebuke and punishment. But in the world of existence, it is only one or some effects, such as some movements made by a human being. The existential or created aspect of this act is caused by external causes, which all boil down to the Original Divine Cause [which is behind every existential reality]. The description of this act as “evil” and its subsequent implications are only a result of some legal or rational classification, but not an existential entity in the external world. Suppose, for

instance, that Zayd is the manager of some organization. “Manager” is a social title that Zayd has in his interactions with us, and because of this title he is entitled to certain privileges such as being respected, being in charge of affairs, and having authority and priority over others. However, in terms of his existential reality, Zayd is only a human like all other humans. There is no difference whatsoever between him as a manager and his subordinates. At this plane there is no such thing as management and its implications. The same goes with other titles such as rich, poor, master, slave, honorable, ignoble, higher-class, lower-class, and numerous other titles.

Overall, even though God’s creation encompasses everything, it applies to the various acts that occur in society only in terms of their external existence and reality. Meanwhile, actions also have another aspect, which is how they are characterized in society as good, evil, obedience, disobedience and other similar labels. This aspect is not subject to creation and

existentiation. These titles and qualities have no existence except in the field of social legislation and assessment, and the plane of mental derivation and convention.

Given the above, it should be clear that conventional titles and classifications—such as command, prohibition, good, evil, obedience, disobedience, reward, punishment, the connection between actions and

their retribution, lordship, servitude, supervision, subordination, honor, dishonor and so on—are not existential entities that are created in the external world, meaning that they are not things that are created and existentiated. Thus it follows that the universality of God’s creation does not necessitate any of the above-mentioned problems which the scholars have posed. For instance, it does not invalidate the system of religious command, prohibition, reward, punishment and so on.

After all, how can someone advocate such duality while God’s Book repeatedly emphasizes the following ideas: (1) He is the Creator of all things; (2) He is the One, the Dominant; (3) His decree, determination, lordship, regulation and existential guidance embrace all things, without falling short of anything; (4) His kingdom, authority, capacity and

rule include all things; and (5) everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, whether apparent or hidden? How can these Qur’anic teachings—which inform us of a monotheistic lordship in the universe— comply with the existence of infinitely many creatures of other creators among His creatures?1

it necessarily means the negation of a causal relationship between other things. There is no cause in the world of existence but God. As with other apparent causes, it is rather God’s ʿādah (habitual custom, common

Whatever its roots may be, this is one of the most baseless illusions and clearly against the Qur’an’s arguments. God proves the Creator’s existence and oneness by referring to His visible signs in the universe, which

means the ongoing system that governs every kind of creature throughout its life, such as the changes and transformations that it goes through, the acts that it does or are done to it, and the benefits that it gives to others or receives from them. Some examples of these signs in the Qur’an are: (1) the sun, the moon, the stars, as well as their rise, fall and the subsequent benefits that people derive from them; (2) the change of seasons in earth; (3) the seas, the rivers and the ships that sail in them; (4) the clouds, the rain and their subsequent benefits for humans, animals and plants; (5) the natural stages of human creation, including sperm, fetus, childhood, youth, maturity and age.

All of these pertain to the continuation and subsistence (baqāʾ) of things, which are identified as the actions and effects of God. At the same time these events are causes for events that occur afterwards and subsequent to them. Today’s events are the causes of tomorrow’s events, just

as they are the effects of yesterday’s events. If these events were needless of God in their subsistence, and if the universe were self-sufficient in pursuing its course by its internal system and set of causes, then none of these Qur’anic arguments and proofs would hold. It should be clarified that the Qur’an pursues two objectives in referring to these signs: (1) to prove God as their cause and agent (fāʿil); and (2) to prove God as their end and goal (ghāyah). Let us will analyze how the Qur’an argues through each of these two channels:

(1) With regards to God being the cause and agent of everything, the Qur’an says: Is there any doubt about Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth? (14:10). It is evident that no being in the contingent world has created itself. Nor has another being like itself given it existence, because that other being would be equally needy of being created. It must be that existence traces back to something that exists by the virtue of itself, such that it cannot possibly be characterized by nonexistence. Otherwise, none of these things would come to existence. Hence, all beings are brought to existence by God Who subsists by Himself, without being subject to any loss or change whatsoever.

However, the beings are not needless of God even after they are created. Existentiation is not like heating and other similar processes. Once

something is warmed up by fire, it retains its heat for while even if the fire is removed. However, if we assume the same thing about existence, then it would mean that once something is given existence, it all of a sudden turns into a necessary being which subsists by itself. An implication of this is that the object cannot possibly be annihilated, because otherwise it would contradict our assumption. This is something that we can understands by our basic and innate human nature (fiṭrah): that if the beings had their existence for themselves and were independent of their Lord in one way or another, then they would never undergo death and decay, because it is impossible for something to rule its own destruction and wretchedness. This idea [that the beings are not independent of God in their subsistence] can be inferred from verses like: Everything is perishing except

His Face (28:88); And they control not for themselves any harm or profit, and they control not death nor life, nor raising (the dead) to life (25:3). This is also referred to by many other verses which state that God is the sole Possessor of all things; there is no other owner for anything; and nothing has any status other than being His property.

Therefore, just as beings receive existence from God at the onset of their creation and origination, they continue to receive existence from Him as long as they live and subsist. A being exists as long as God bestows existence upon it; but the moment God cuts offHis bestowment, the name of that thing is wiped offfrom the tablet of existents. God says: All do We aid—these as well as those—out of the bounty of your Lord, and the bounty of your Lord is not confined (17:20). There are many more verses in this regard.

(2) The idea that God is the end and goal of everything is found in verses which describe the uniform and harmonious system which governs the universe. The beings and events in the universe are ordered as a

congruous chain, such that when one member of this system advances toward its perfection and happiness, it also helps the other members to advance. For example, human beings benefit from the system which governs the animals and plants. Similarly, plants benefit from the system that

governs the earth and the atmosphere. Earthly beings benefit from the heavenly beings and vice versa. This means that all beings in the universe are incorporated in a single connected system which moves every species toward its existential perfection and bliss. If one’s reason is awake and his innate human nature remains unadulterated, then the person will only conclude that all this must be by the design and direction of a Planner Who is certainly Mighty, Knowledgeable, Wise and Aware.

This design and direction is based on creating, existentiating and fashioning the essence, being and identity of every thing in a mold that determines its effects and keeps it on its desired track from the onset of its creation throughout the stages of its journey that are planned for it, until the point where it is supposed to end. The existents carry through these stages while being mounted on means and instruments, driven from behind by God’s measurement (qadar), and led from the front by His decree (qaḍāʾ).1 The Qur’an says: Surely His is the creation and the command (7:54); Surely His is the judgment (6:62); And everyone has a direction to which he turns (2:148); And Allah judges; there is no repeller of His

judgment (13:41); He Who watches over every soul as to what it earns (13:33). How can someone contemplate the likes of these verses [which are many] and then turn them away from their clear and explicit meaning? That would be the case if one has the following view of the creation: God only created the beings at the first stage, but then lefiithem on their own and sat aside watching them, like a retired architect. After all, what else could He do beyond that stage? Then

the beings started to move around and interact with each other according to causal relationships between them, while being independent as causes and effects. This is all while their Creator is watching them on the side and awaiting the day when all of them perish, so that He may give them a new creation where He rewards those who listened to His call in their life, and punishes those who arrogantly defied Him. Before then He simply tolerates their mischief, except that sometimes His wrath is kindled

because of what He sees from some of them, whereby He prevents them from what they wish to do and stops their plots as a barrier and opponent that works parallel to them at the same level.

What this means is that God steps in and stops being an impartial spectator in certain cases that the independent set of causes and effects in the universe pursues a goal that displeases Him or does not please Him. Thus He interrupts the causes at work in the world by creating His

desired outcome. This can only be by suspending the law of causality in that certain case, because if He brings about what He wants through the ordinary causes and means, then the outcome would be an effect of the causes at work in the universe, not an effect of God.

In the same light, these thinkers have insisted that things like miracles and supernatural acts occur only by God’s will, without complying with the universal law of causality. This reduces to negating the law of causality in the universe, which negates their initial belief that all things need

God for their origination, but not for their subsistence.

Hence, these thinkers must choose one of two views:

(1) The universe is completely needless of God; it operates independently by its own orderly system; and He has no impact in any part of it

or any event that happens in it. The only need of the universe to God was for its initial origination, but now that it has been created, it no longer depends on Him.

(2) God is the Creator of anything which can be called a “thing”

The reader should realize by now that the Qur’an rejects the first view because there are many verses which talk about the applicability of God’s creation to everything, and His invisible dominance over the outward, inward, beginning and end of every being and event, both in origination and subsistence. Therefore, the Qur’an leaves us only with the second view, which is also confirmed by a meticulous rational discussion [which we presented above].
